hint: The derivative of $\tan x$ is $\sec^2 x$. With an inside function, multiply by the derivative of the inside as well.

hints.text: The derivative of $\tan x$ is $\sec^2 x$. With an inside function, multiply by the derivative of the inside as well.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: $\frac{d}{dx}\tan x$ at $x = \frac{\pi}{4}$ is $\sec^2\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{1}{\cos^2(\pi/4)} = \frac{1}{1/2} = 2$. Now the inside is $2x$, so expect one more factor.
The chain rule gives $f'(x) = \sec^2(2x) \cdot 2 = 2\sec^2(2x)$. At $x = \frac{\pi}{8}$ the inside angle is $\frac{\pi}{4}$, so evaluate the secant squared there.

explanation: The outside $\tan u$ has derivative $\sec^2 u$, and the inside $u = 2x$ has derivative $2$. So $f'(x) = 2\sec^2(2x)$.
At $x = \frac{\pi}{8}$ the angle is $2x = \frac{\pi}{4}$ and $\cos\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, so $\sec^2\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{1}{1/2} = 2$.
So $f'\left(\frac{\pi}{8}\right) = 2 \cdot 2 = 4$. Dropping the chain factor gives $2$, half the true slope.

alternativeExplanations.title: Derive $\sec^2$ with the quotient rule
steps: $\tan u = \frac{\sin u}{\cos u}$, so $\frac{d}{du}\tan u = \frac{\cos u \cdot \cos u - \sin u \cdot (-\sin u)}{\cos^2 u} = \frac{\cos^2 u + \sin^2 u}{\cos^2 u} = \frac{1}{\cos^2 u}$.
With $u = 2x$ the chain rule adds a factor $2$: $f'(x) = \frac{2}{\cos^2(2x)}$.
